paper_title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: LLM agents increasingly call tools whose outputs are long, such as logs, search results, and simulator reports. harness must choose how such output reaches the model: paste it into the context, truncated to fixed budget (inline), or save it to file 1 that the agent reads through an outline, search tool, or ranged reads (retrieval). File-based delivery can reduce context usage by loading selected portions on demand (Rajasekaran et al., 2025). Yet Sen et al. (2026) find that delivering search results as files lowers accuracy in most of the harness model pairs they test, without identifying why, and models do not always use context that contains everything they need (Xie et al., 2026; Joren et al., 2025). What remains unknown is where the loss arises: wrong answer rarely shows whether the agent computed the wrong value, never saw the right one, or saw it and still answered wrongly. deterministic simulator makes this observable. We study LLM agents operating PHREEQC, an aqueous-geochemistry simulator (Parkhurst and Appelo, 2013) whose section-structured reports reach 846.8k characters, on 158 multiple-choice items whose answer keys we re-verified by execution (Section 2.1). We change only how the simulators report reaches the agent: inline, or as table of contents (TOC) of its sections from which the agent reads line ranges. We re-run every input an agent wrote and search every tool result it received, and so tell for each trajectory whether its simulation produced the keyed value (build), whether the value reached the agent (exposure), and whether the agent then answered correctly from it (closure). Each stage points to different remedy: build defect to better simulation inputs, an exposure or closure loss to change in what and how the agent reads. We therefore first locate the loss and then test the location by intervening on that stage. Four results follow. 1. The cost of retrieval depends on the model. Pooled over runs, TOC changes accuracy relative to inline output by 0.6 to +0.2 pp for Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and GPT-5.4, with intervals that include zero, and by 11.3 and 7.9 pp for GPT-5.1 and GPTFigure 1: Same simulation, different evidence (item 121, GPT-5.1). The agents simulation writes the keyed value to the report, at the options precision, and to its own output file, with more digits. Under TOC the agent reads only its own file and truncates 2.75065 to the distractor 2.750 (evidence substitution), even when told how to round; told to answer from the report, it answers correctly. Right: for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, report skipping over all 158 items, and wrong answers once the keyed value is seen (100 minus closure) on the 137 numeric items. 5.2. Keyword search, which uses no simulatorspecific structure, does no better (Section 3).

sections.title: Items and Verification
sections.content: 2. The loss lies in what agents read, not in what they compute. GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 produce the keyed value about equally often under every interface. Under retrieval, however, they often skip the report and answer from their own SELECTED_OUTPUT files, which print more digits, and they truncate such values to neighboring option in about three of four cases. We call this evidence substitution (Figure 1). Holding the simulation fixed and changing only the delivery, TOC still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 pp (Section 4). 3. null net effect can hide the loss. GPT-5.4 substitutes evidence too and loses about ten points to it on numeric items, but computes the keyed value more often under retrieval, so its net change is indistinguishable from zero. 4. Intervening on what agents read removes the closure loss. An instruction to answer from the report cuts report skipping to under 2% and raises closure to 99% without changing build; relative to all TOC runs, accuracy rises by +6.3 (GPT-5.1), +7.9 (GPT-5.2), and +7.8 pp (GPT5.4). Inlining reports that fit has the same effect; an instruction that only asks for correct rounding has none (Section 5). We use the four-option multiple-choice items of Zhang et al. (2026b), written by one domain expert. Each describes PHREEQC simulation setup and asks for one quantity from its output (a pH at reaction step, saturation index, molality in transport cell); several items share setup. Reference answers come from PHREEQC 3.8.6 with fixed, author-supplied phreeqc.dat. For numeric items, distractors typically differ from the key in the last printed digit, so they can be answered only by computing the value, not by estimating it; the remaining items ask for comparison, name, or count. Answer-key verification. We re-executed all 200 items of the original pool, using the authors own input where available (9 of 20 setups) and otherwise literal encoding of the item text with PHREEQC defaults, never adjusting an input toward the key. An item is retained only if the printed value matches the keyed option exactly and uniquely and does not change under tighter convergence or alternative step-size settings. 158 items from 19 setups qualify. The item author confirmed each of the 42 excluded items as defective (an incorrect key, numerically unstable redox quantity, or defective wording). Exclusion never used model outputs. All main-text results use the 158 items; Appendix gives the procedure and shows that the full pool leads to the same conclusions.

sections.title: 2.2 Agents and Output Delivery
sections.content: Each agent has four tools write_file, read_file (optionally with line range), list_file, and execute_phreeqc and works in an isolated workspace for at most 24 steps, committing to an answer by writing it to file. PHREEQC writes formatted report (result.out) that prints each quantity at the precision the answer options use; agents may also add SELECTED_OUTPUT or USER_PUNCH blocks, which write chosen quantities to separate files with more digits. The conditions differ in what execute_phreeqc returns and in the system-prompt line that describes it (Appendix B). Raw100k (inline) returns the report, head/tailtruncated to 100,000 characters. TOC returns metadata and an index of report sections with starting lines; the agent reads line ranges. Grep returns metadata only; the agent finds evidence with regular-expression search tool. Hybrid returns the report inline when it fits within 100,000 characters and the TOC otherwise. TOC+Report and TOC+Round add three-sentence instruction to TOC, to answer from the report or to round to the options precision (Section 5). We evaluate Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash Preview through their APIs: the Claude models at temperature 0 without extended thinking, the GPT and Gemini models at API defaults with no reasoning-effort setting. Direct and chain-ofthought (CoT) prompting without tools serve as no-tool baselines. Runs. Each model has one headline run with Raw100k and one with TOC. We rerun TOC three times for Sonnet and the GPT models and Raw100k once for the GPT models, and run Grep and the interventions (Section 5) on subset of models; Table 8 lists every run. For the 33 items whose report exceeds 100k characters, all four TOC runs use one run with fixed index, as the original index was empty for such reports. Rates are averaged over runs; counts use each trajectory once. Our primary comparison is TOC against inline per model, with every run pooled per item, 95% itembootstrap intervals, and sign-flip permutation tests Holm-corrected over the five models.

sections.title: 2.3 Locating Where an Agent Fails
sections.content: For every full-agent trajectory with complete log (5,773) we rebuilt each input the agent executed and re-ran it offline with the same binary and database: 11,007 simulator calls in all. For numeric trajectories with last execution available for comparison, re-running that execution reproduces its stored report in 4,971 of 5,009 cases; the rest differ only in line order. For the 137 items with numeric answers we then ask three questions, matching values at the precision the options are printed with: Build (p): did any of the agents own simulations print the keyed value? Exposure (s): given that it was produced, did the value reach the agent, inline or through read or search result? Closure (c): given that the agent saw the value, did it answer correctly? Accuracy decomposes exactly as plus the accuracy of answers given without the keyed value in view (unsupported: nearest-option picks and guesses). We attribute each conditions accuracy change relative to the same models logged inline run to these four factors with Shapley decomposition and 95% item-bootstrap intervals; the decomposition allocates an observed difference among the stages and does not estimate independent causal effects. We also record the file from which each seen value came. Matching is numeric, so printed number counts as the keyed value wherever it appears; automatic and manual stage labels agree on 52 of 58 numeric trajectories read by hand, and the results hold on the 93 numeric items whose keyed value occurs only once in the reference report (Appendix C).

sections.title: 4 Agents Answer from Their Own Output
sections.content: What the agents compute does not change detectably. Within each of GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1, the share of trajectories whose own simulation produces the keyed value (p) is similar under every interface  (Table 3)  , and the build term of the accuracy change stays within 2 pp, with intervals that include zero. The loss persists with the simulation held fixed. To separate delivery from computation, we freeze GPT-5.2s logged inline run at its first successful execution on 131 numeric items and continue the same visible history twice, once with the report inline and once with the TOC (Appendix D). Both arms share the files, system prompt, reading tools, and remaining turns; they can read files and submit an answer but not rerun the simulator. Over three paired repeats, TOC changes accuracy by 9.4 pp [14.5, 4.6], and the interval also excludes zero when setups are resampled. The loss is as large on the 115 reports that fit inline and on the 84 items whose frozen report contains the keyed value (10.1 and 9.9 pp). The loss lies in exposure and closure. For GPT5.2 under TOC, closure accounts for 7.7 of the 11.4 pp change on numeric items, with an interval that excludes zero, and exposure for 2.5 pp. For GPT-5.1 the loss splits about evenly between exposure and closure, each with an interval that excludes zero (Tables 3 and 9). Grep shows the same pattern. These totals are relative to the single logged inline run and cover numeric items only, so they differ from the pooled contrast in Table 1. Under retrieval, agents substitute their own output for the report. Under TOC, GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 receive no part of the simulators report in 60.3% and 53.0% of trajectories and most of them read one of their own selected-output files instead  (Table 4)  . They define such files about as often inline, but there the report is already in context and they answer from it. We call this evidence substitution: answering from output the agent defined itself instead of the tools canonical report. The term is descriptive: agents may read these files simply because they are short. Sonnet skips the report in only 10.5% of TOC trajectories. 4 Table 2: Accuracy over runs on the 158 verified items. The report prints each quantity at the precision the options use, whereas selectedoutput files print more digits, so an agent reading them must round, and the GPT models often truncate instead. When an agent saw value that rounds to the key but truncates to neighboring option, GPT-5.2 chose the neighbor in 26/35 TOC trajectories and GPT-5.1 in 19/27, against 1/35 for Sonnet. Accordingly, answers were nearly always correct when the keyed value was seen as the report prints it, and correct in only 72.5% (GPT-5.2) and 66.3% (GPT-5.1) of trajectories that saw it only with more digits. With both forms in view, 19 of 20 answers were correct; errors concentrate where the more precise form is the only one in view. This comparison is observational, since trajectories of the two kinds can differ in their items; Section tests the link by intervention. Exposure. When the keyed value was produced but never seen, the agent had almost always received no part of the report (14 of 17 cases for GPT-5.1, 6 of 7 for GPT-5.2): its own output printed stand-in quantity, such as log activity, and the agent answered from it. sections.title: Intervening on What Agents Read
sections.content: If the loss arises because agents answer from their own higher-precision files, changing only what they read should remove it without changing what they compute. We test two interventions and one control instruction against TOC control  (Table 5)  . TOC+Report adds three sentences to the TOC tool description and to every tool result: the values in result.out are authoritative and printed at the options precision; the agent should take the value from the relevant section of result.out and not answer from selected-output files, which print unrounded values that can match neighboring option (verbatim in Appendix B). Hybrid adds no instruction and inlines reports that fit within 100,000 characters. The instruction changes what agents read and removes the closure loss. With the instruction, report skipping falls to 0.0% (GPT-5.2) and 1.6% (GPT-5.1), the agents rarely read their own output files, and 99% of their correct numeric answers that saw the keyed value took it from the report. Closure rises to 98.8% and 99.2%, no trajectory falls into the truncation trap, and build is unchanged within run-to-run variation  (Table 5)  . Accuracy rises over all five TOC runs by +7.9 and +6.3 pp (+7.1 pp [+1.9, +12.4] averaged over the two models) and over the TOC control by +3.5 and +7.9 pp, 6 comparison limited by one control run per model. GPT-5.2 reaches its inline accuracy; GPT-5.1 remains below it (5.1 pp [11.4, +0.9]), with the residual in the build, exposure, and unsupported terms rather than in closure. rounding instruction alone does not help. To separate the source from the precision step, TOC+Round replaces the instruction with three sentences that ask the agent to round values with more digits than the options to the nearest value at the options precision, never truncating, and name no file. Agents still skip the report about as often as under TOC and closure stays at about 82%  (Table 5)  ; they still choose the truncated neighbor in 17/25 and 14/19 trap cases, although told not to truncate. Accuracy changes by only +0.6 and +1.2 pp relative to all TOC runs, and TOC+Report exceeds TOC+Round by +7.3 pp [+0.6, +13.9] and +5.1 pp [1.6, +12.0]. Telling the agents how to round does not stop the misrounding; directing them to the value already printed at the right precision does. The instruction also lifts GPT-5.4. With the instruction, GPT-5.4 reaches 81.6% in both runs, +7.8 pp [+2.2, +13.6] above its TOC runs and +7.9 pp [+2.5, +13.3] above its inline runs. Report skipping falls to 0.0% and closure rises to 99.0%, and the build gain of retrieval remains (+3.4 pp relative to inline), so the instruction removes the evidence-use loss while keeping what retrieval adds. Inlining what fits has the same effect. Over three runs, Hybrid raises accuracy over the TOC control by +4.6 (GPT-5.2) and +8.0 pp (GPT-5.1). Report skipping nearly disappears and closure returns to its inline level  (Table 5)  . Relative to the inline runs, GPT-5.2 changes by +1.2 pp and GPT5.1 by 5.0 pp, again with GPT-5.1s residual outside closure. What the interventions establish. Both interventions restore closure without changing build, and for GPT-5.2 the paired replay shows the loss with computation fixed. Together, these results place the cost of retrieval in which evidence the agent answers from. Hybrid needs no knowledge of the tool; the instruction keeps retrieval but must name the canonical output. sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: Retrieval adds choice of evidence. Our interfaces are information-equivalent: every number in the inline report is one read away, and for GPT-5.2, with the simulation held fixed, the loss remains on reports that fit inline. What differs is the information bounded agent can use (Xu et al., 2020). Retrieval turns reading the report into choice of evidence. Inline, one source is in view; under retrieval, the report competes with the files the agent wrote itself, and models that choose badly lose accuracy. The instruction works because it makes that choice for them. This also reconciles our results with work in which retrieval helps weaker models most (Li et al., 2025): there pipeline selects the evidence; here the model does. Implications for harness design. Output delivery should be validated for each model harness serves, and by where accuracy is lost rather than by final accuracy alone, since net effect near zero can hide an evidence-use loss. Inlining outputs that fit is safe default; when agents can create their own outputs, harness should state which output is authoritative, which in our setting also reduces input tokens.

sections.title: 7 Related Work
sections.content: Delivering tool output to agents. The agent computer interface, including how files are viewed and searched, changes what software-engineering agents achieve (Yang et al., 2024). Harnesses handle long tool outputs by truncating, masking, or compressing observations (Lindenbauer et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025), or by writing them to files that the agent opens or searches (Abramovich et al., 2025; Rajasekaran et al., 2025); long responses also degrade function calling (Kate et al., 2025). Closest to our work, Sen et al. (2026) find that file-based delivery of search results lowers accuracy in nine of ten harnessmodel pairs, frontier models included, and hypothesize readintegrateretry cycle as the cause. On the items we use, Zhang et al. (2026b) report that table-of-contents interface lowers the accuracy of some models; we verify the answer keys, find the cost to be model-dependent, locate it within individual trajectories, and test the location by intervention. Sufficient versus usable information. Shannon information does not depend on how signal is encoded, but the information computationally bounded observer can use does (Xu et al., 2020). Xie et al. (2026) show that messages preserving all decision-relevant information can fail bounded receivers, and decompose the loss into externalization, absorption, and action closure. Joren et al. (2025) find that smaller models often fail to use sufficient retrieved context, and search agents answer far better from the gold documents than by searching for them (Chen et al., 2025). deterministic simulator has no externalization loss, and our exposure and closure stages correspond to absorption and closure. 7 Locating agent failures. Agent failures are usually attributed by human or model judges (Zhang et al., 2025), or by counterfactual replay that labels data for learned attributor (Zhang et al., 2026a); RAG diagnostics separate retriever from generator errors against reference claims (Ru et al., 2024). Agents for scientific software are usually studied on one package and graded on outcomes: OpenFOAM cases that run (Yue et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2024), COMSOL targets (Mudur et al., 2025), or molecular-dynamics subtasks (Campbell et al., 2025); SUPER checks whether expected outputs appear in executed cells (Bogin et al., 2024). Reexecuting the agents own inputs with deterministic simulator gives every stage ground-truth answer without judge. Models prefer self-generated over retrieved context (Tan et al., 2024) and round to significant digits unreliably (Yang et al., 2025), which makes the failure we find plausible; we show that an interface choice triggers it.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: On 158 PHREEQC items, retrieving the simulators report instead of inlining it costs GPT-5.1 and GPT5.2 accuracy and shows no detectable net cost for the Claude models and GPT-5.4. Re-executing every logged trajectory shows that the GPT models compute the keyed value but answer from their own higher-precision output and misround it, and that in GPT-5.4 better computation masks this loss; for GPT-5.2, holding the simulation fixed confirms that the loss comes from the delivery. Naming the authoritative output, or inlining reports that fit, removes the closure loss; asking for correct rounding does not. Deterministic tools make such losses visible where final accuracy hides them.

sections.title: 9 Limitations
sections.content: Models. All models are closed and accessed through their APIs. Evidence substitution appears in all three GPT models and rarely in Claude Sonnet 4.6, the Claude model with full trajectory logs; we do not determine which model property drives this difference. Decoding and prompts. The Claude agents ran at temperature 0 without extended thinking, and the GPT and Gemini agents at API defaults with no reasoning-effort setting, so we do not know whether the effect persists with explicit reasoning. The full-agent conditions differ in the systemprompt line that describes the tools return value, and the two instruction conditions also repeat their instruction in every tool result; the paired replay uses the same prompt in both arms. We test one wording of each instruction. Runs. Because of the API budget, not every model was run, repeated, or logged in every condition, so some table cells are empty; Table 8 lists every run. The full-agent conditions were run at different times, and we do not model possible changes in the served models between runs. The four TOC runs share one run on the 33 long-output items and the decomposition uses one logged inline run per model. The paired replay covers GPT-5.2 and starts from checkpoints of its inline run. What verification establishes. retained items key is reproduced by PHREEQC under the authors input or literal encoding of the item text; this is not an independent scientific review of each question. In three setups (24 retained items) the text does not fully specify the reference input; excluding these items leaves 134 items and the same conclusions (Appendix A).

sections.title: A Item Verification
sections.content: Procedure. Every item in the 200-item authorwritten pool was re-executed in PHREEQC 3.8.6 with the frozen phreeqc.dat. For the 9 setups where the authors original PHREEQC input was available we ran it unchanged, adding only output statements; for the remaining setups we encoded the item text literally with PHREEQC defaults (mmol/kgw, 25 C, pe 4 unless stated). Inputs were never adjusted toward the key; where nothing matched, small number of documented alternative readings (step numbering, units, charge balance) were tried and recorded. For redox-sensitive quantities in systems without redox couple, we re-ran with tighter convergence tolerance and alternative step-size and kinetic-integrator settings, and marked an item unstable if the printed value changed at the digit that separates the options. An item is retained only if its printed value matches the keyed option exactly and uniquely and is stable. Model results played no part in this process. Table 6 lists the excluded items; the item author reviewed all of them and agreed that each is defective as written. Table 6: Excluded items by reason (dataset item IDs).

sections.content: 42 Results by item set. Table 7 compares the full pool, the 158 verified items used in the main text, and stricter subset of 134 items that also drops the 24 retained items whose setup text under-specifies the reference input. Accuracies rise when defective items are removed, because models were often marked wrong on items whose key or wording was defective, but the ordering of models and the pattern of TOC versus Raw100k (no detectable difference for the Claude models and GPT-5.4, loss for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2) are the same in all three. Prompts, Tool Results, and Conditions Prompts and tool definitions. Each full agent receives system prompt, the item as its user prompt, and four tool definitions through the API (Figure 2); Grep adds fifth, and the definitions are otherwise the same in every condition. Across conditions, the system prompt changes only in its execute_phreeqc line (Figure 3) and in the mode named in its last line. The no-tool baselines send the item text alone with one of two system prompts (Figure 2). The inline description discourages additional reads, and the retrieval descriptions require them; part of the difference in reading behavior between inline and retrieval conditions may therefore be induced by the descriptions rather than by the return value alone; the paired replay, whose arms share one system prompt, still shows the loss (Appendix D). The TOC+Report instruction both names the authoritative file and gives reason to prefer it; TOC+Round gives only the rounding rule and names no file. Tool results. Every execute_phreeqc call returns the exit status, the last 4,000 characters of PHREEQCs standard output and error, and the names and sizes of the files the run created. Raw100k adds the report, cut to its first and last 50,000 characters with truncation marker when it is longer than 100,000. TOC adds an index of the reports dash-delimited section headers with their starting lines, at most 50 entries (the first and last 25 when report has more), and the hint Use read_file with start_line/end_line to read specific sections. In the headline TOC runs and the TOC reruns the index was empty for reports longer than 100,000 characters, so on those items all four TOC runs use one separate run with the index built; all other runs build it for every report (Section 2.2). TOC+Report and TOC+Round return the TOC payload with their instruction appended to the hint, so the agent sees the instruction in the system prompt and again in every execute_phreeqc result. With line range, read_file returns the requested lines; without one it returns file of up to 20,000 characters whole and otherwise its first and last 80 lines (no content in Grep). An example trajectory. Figure 4 abridges GPT5.1 TOC trajectory on item 121, the item of Figure 1. The agent defines selected-output file in its first input, reads that file after the run, and answers with the truncation of the value it prints. It never opens result.out, although the index points to the section that prints the keyed value. The intervention runs. The intervention and TOC control runs used the same harness, item file, and step budget, with the index built for every report size. TOC+Round reached 62.0% and 57.0% for GPT-5.2 and 55.7% and 57.6% for GPT-5.1. TOC+Report reached 67.1% and 66.5% for GPT5.2, 62.7% and 60.8% for GPT-5.1, and 81.6% and 81.6% for GPT-5.4 in its two runs; GPT-5.4s logged inline run reached 76.6%. With the instruction, GPT-5.4 defined selected-output file in only 3.8% of trajectories (83.3% under TOC), and 100.0% of its correct numeric answers that saw the keyed value took it from the report (63.9% under TOC). Of the correct numeric answers that saw the keyed value, the share that saw it in the report rather than only in the agents own selected-output files was 40.8% (GPT-5.2) and 68.0% (GPT-5.1) in the TOC control, 99.4% and 99.2% with the instruction, 92.5% and 99.0% under Hybrid, and 98.8% and 100.0% in the inline runs. Accuracy gains under the instruction therefore come from answers taken from the report, not from correctly rounded selected-output values. For GPT-5.2, Hybrid used 59.7k input tokens per item, against 61.8k 11 under TOC and 65.7k inline, with the saving relative to inline coming from long outputs. GPT-5.1s Hybrid runs used far fewer tokens (28.3k per item), mostly because the agent rarely read an optional database reference file that it read in about two thirds of its other TOC and inline runs; the TOC control run also used fewer tokens (34.2k), so we do not claim this as saving of Hybrid. Mean input tokens per item under the instruction were 58.0k (control) and 49.7k (instruction) for GPT-5.2, and 34.2k and 30.8k for GPT-5.1.

Use read_file only if you need to inspect an additional output file or re-read specific portion. TOC: Run PHREEQC on an input file. Returns metadata and TOC for result.out. Independently of the automatic labels, we read 68 trajectories: 12 TOC losses each for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 (items wrong under TOC but correct inline, each read together with the inline trajectory), 6 Grep losses for GPT-5.2, and 8 Sonnet TOC failures. Losses selected on the outcome are therefore dominated by build failures that churn between runs and net out, which is why we rely on the decomposition rather than on item-level losses. On the 58 numeric trajectories in this sample, the automatic stage (build, exposure, closure, or correct with the keyed value in view) agrees with the manual one in 52 cases. sections.title: Fixed
sections.content: Checkpoints. We take the first execution returning exit code zero in GPT-5.2s logged inline run, before its result reaches the model. Of the 137 numeric items, 131 have such checkpoint; the remaining six have no successful execution. Selection uses the execution status, independently of the original final answer or whether the output contains the keyed value. We reconstruct the visible history and workspace by replaying the preceding file writes and PHREEQC calls in order, including earlier failed executions. For the 115 untruncated reports, re-execution matches the recorded report after normalizing path and timing lines and separator rules; the other 16 original returns contain only the capped head and tail. Both delivery arms use the same reconstructed files, verified by hashes. Paired continuations. Only the pending execution result differs: Raw100k returns the report inline with the usual 100,000-character cap, whereas TOC returns its section index, built at every report size. The arms share common system prompt, the visible history, file-reading tools, and the remaining budget of 24 assistant turns, where is the executions turn. They can list or read the frozen files and submit final_answer.txt; simulation files remain fixed. We run 3 continuations per item and condition with GPT-5.2s API defaults and 4,096-completion-token cap per call. Item order and the order of the two arms within each pair are shuffled with fixed seed (20261011), and the paired arms run consecutively. The 115 frozen reports that fit inline yield 75.4% inline and 65.2% under TOC (10.1 pp). For the 16 longer reports the corresponding accuracies are 41.7% and 37.5%. Using the matching rule in Appendix C, the keyed value is present in the frozen report for 84 items; accuracy on these items is 93.7% inline and 83.7% under TOC. The fixed outputs therefore retain the same value while the delivery choice changes how often the agent answers correctly.
